name: Seiyunchin (Seiunchin)
description: Seiyunchin was introduced in Okinawa by Kanryo Higaonna. He learned the kata from Ryu Ryu Ko. The original creator of the kata is unknown. Seiyunchin means “control and push”. This corresponds to unbalancing (or pulling) someone, controlling and attacking with a short-distance technique (attack to a vital point, throw, joint lock). Seiyunchin is the kata in which you develop a lot of “chiru no chan chan” - push-off power or explosive power. The kata has a large number of movements over a considerable distance, both forwards and backwards. Additionally, the kata contains a large number of techniques performed in shiko dachi (see the gedan barai in Gekisai dai ichi for points of attention). During a movement from shiko dachi to shiko dachi, the body remains low and the feet slide across the floor. In the kata, shiko dachi occurs several times, but each time the way the movement takes place and how the power is delivered is different.

origin.title: Origin
origin.content: Seiyunchin was introduced in Okinawa by Kanryo Higaonna. He learned the kata from Ryu Ryu Ko.

transmission.title: Transmission to Goju-Ryu
transmission.content: Miyagi Sensei introduced Seiyunchin into the Goju-ryu syllabus and taught it to his students.

historicalDevelopment.title: Historical Development
historicalDevelopment.content: Within Goju-Ryu, Seiyunchin has remained virtually unchanged; variations are limited to interpretation of grips.

technicalFeatures.title: Technical and Philosophical Characteristics
technicalFeatures.content: The kata has a large number of movements over a considerable distance, both forwards and backwards. Additionally, the kata contains a large number of techniques performed in shiko dachi.

controversy.title: Controversy/Variations within Goju-Ryu
controversy.content: There are small interpretation differences (open or closed fist usage) but no major controversies.

relationships.title: Relationship to other kata/Systems
relationships.content: Seiyunchin is closely related to Naha-te kata through the use of tension and heiho.

modernPractice.title: Use in Modern Practice
modernPractice.content: Seiyunchin is seen in the dojo as a powerful conditioning kata, suitable for training grip and core strength.
